This is where the Club Infinite quietly pulls ahead. 5X on United, 2X on dining and all other travel. Everything else earns 1X, so it's not a catch-all card — but the Delta Reserve and Citi Executive both earn a pathetic 1X on dining and most non-airline travel, so the Club Infinite is earning double what its competitors do in two of the biggest everyday categories. For a premium airline card, that's a real edge.

PQP earning: 1 PQP per $15 spent on all purchases, up to 28,000 PQP per year. That cap is absurd — 28,000 PQP is the entire PQP-only bar for Premier 1K (Premier Platinum takes 18,000), and the 1,500 annual bonus PQP sit on top of the cap. You still need four United flight segments a year for any Premier tier, and maxing the cap takes $420,000 in spend, but if you're chasing Premier 1K, this card does more heavy lifting than any other.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
Full MileagePlus redemption access — and the miles you earn here go far:

  • United and Star Alliance flights: Book across 25+ airlines — ANA, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, EVA Air, and more. The sweet spots are legendary.
  • Cardmember award pricing: At least 10% fewer miles than non-cardmembers pay on United and United Express award flights (at least 15% fewer once you have Premier status). Partner awards don't get the discount.
  • United TravelBank: Convert miles to travel credits
  • Upgrades: Cabin upgrades on select routes
  • Hotels, car rentals, merchandise: Through the MileagePlus portal. Lower value — use for flights instead.

The up to 20,000-mile award flight discount (earned at $20K and $40K spending thresholds) isn't unique to the Club Infinite (the Quest gets a 10,000-mile discount each anniversary plus another at $20K spend, and the Explorer gets one at $20K spend), but it provides excellent value, especially on premium cabin redemptions where every mile saved is worth more.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
• United Club membership: Unlimited access to 45+ United Club lounges worldwide for you and one adult guest. Standalone value ~$750/year. This is the whole reason most people get this card.
  • $240/year Instacart credits: Two $10 credits per month + complimentary Instacart+ membership. If you use Instacart, this is basically free groceries.
  • $150/year rideshare credits: $12/month (Jan-Nov), $18 in December. Take Ubers, get money back.
  • $200/year Renowned Hotels credits: Statement credits on prepaid hotel stays booked through the Renowned Hotels portal. Requires using a specific booking channel.
  • Up to 20,000-mile award flight discount: 10,000 at $20K spend + 10,000 at $40K spend per year. A reward for high spenders.
  • 1,500 PQP annual bonus + up to 28,000 PQP from spending
  • Up to $100/year Avis/Budget credits: $50 in United TravelBank cash on each of your first two Avis or Budget rentals booked through cars.united.com.
  • Up to $200/year JSX credits: Statement credits on JSX flight bookings.
  • 2 free checked bags on United flights
  • Premier Access: Priority check-in, security, and boarding. The full VIP treatment.

Total quantifiable annual credit value (excluding lounge membership): $890. Including the Club membership value: $1,640+. Even if you only use half the credits, the card pays for itself through lounge access alone.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:
• United Club regulars — if you'd buy a membership anyway (~$750/year), this card is essentially free with up to $890 in credits on top. No-brainer territory.

  • Frequent diners and travelers — 2X on dining and all non-United travel, 5X on United. Everything else earns 1X, so pair it with a flat-rate card for the rest.
  • Travelers who use Instacart, rideshare, and hotels regularly — up to $590/year in credits that fit naturally into most people's lives (and $890 once you add JSX and Avis/Budget).

Who should pass: travelers who rarely use United Clubs (you're paying for access you won't use — the biggest waste in credit cards), anyone who flies United infrequently, or budget-conscious travelers who can't justify $695 even with credits. If you don't need the lounge, the Quest at $350 delivers most of the same benefits at half the cost. Don't buy aspiration — buy what you'll actually use.

title: Capital One Quicksilver
scouts_verdict:
The Quicksilver isn't going to make anyone's heart race, and that's exactly the point. It's the credit card equivalent of a reliable friend — always there, never costs you anything, and quietly has your back when things go wrong.

At 1.5% flat cash back, it loses the pure earning rate fight to the Active Cash and Double Cash at 2%. On $20,000 in annual spending, that's $100 you're leaving on the table. But those cards charge 3% on foreign transactions, which means one international trip can erase months of extra cash back. The Quicksilver's no-FTF policy and travel insurance suite — baggage delay, lost luggage, trip cancellation — give it a real edge that doesn't show up in a simple rate comparison.

The bottom line: if you never travel and want maximum cash back, get the Active Cash. But if you want a zero-cost, zero-hassle card that works everywhere in the world and protects you when stuff goes sideways, the Quicksilver is the one. It won't win any awards, but it'll never let you down.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Capital One Quicksilver Cash Rewards Credit Card is the Honda Civic of credit cards. It's not flashy, it won't win any races, but it's reliable, costs nothing to own, and does exactly what you need without any drama. Unlimited 1.5% cash back on every purchase. $0 annual fee. No categories to track, no quarterly activations, no mental overhead.

Is 1.5% the highest flat rate out there? Nope — the Wells Fargo Active Cash and Citi Double Cash both offer 2%. But here's where the Quicksilver fights back: no foreign transaction fees and a surprisingly robust set of travel protections (baggage delay, lost luggage, trip cancellation) that those 2% cards don't have. If you ever leave the country or want that coverage without paying for it, the Quicksilver earns its spot in your wallet.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• Unlimited 1.5% cash back on every purchase — no categories, no caps, no thinking required.
  • $0 annual fee — free to hold, forever.
  • No foreign transaction fees — a genuine rarity among no-annual-fee cash back cards. Use it in Paris, Tokyo, wherever.
  • 5% cash back on hotels, rental cars and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel.
  • 5% cash back on purchases through Capital One Entertainment.
  • Travel accident insurance when you book with the card.
  • Rental car insurance — collision and theft coverage on rentals charged to the card. This alone can save you $15-$30/day at the rental counter.
  • Baggage delay insurance — up to $100/day for 3 days when bags are 4+ hours late.
  • Lost/damaged luggage coverage — up to $3,000 per trip when you put the fare on the card.
  • Purchase protection — covers damage or theft of new purchases for 90 days, up to $1,000 per claim ($25,000 per 12 months).
  • Extended warranty on eligible purchases.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:

Zero annual fee. Zero foreign transaction fees. This card costs you absolutely nothing to own and use anywhere on the planet. Capital One is one of the few issuers that charges no FTF across its entire card lineup — they deserve credit for that (no pun intended).

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn a one-time $200 cash bonus after spending $500 on purchases within the first 3 months from account opening. You're not eligible if you've received a Quicksilver new-cardmember bonus in the past 48 months.

A $500 spend threshold is about as low as it gets — you'll hit that through normal living without trying. The $200 bonus matches the Freedom Unlimited and beats the Active Cash's current $100. Nothing extraordinary, but easy money.

sections.title: Earning Rates
sections.content:
CategoryEarn Rate
All purchases1.5% cash back
Capital One Travel bookings (hotels, rental cars, vacation rentals)5% cash back
Capital One Entertainment purchases5% cash back

Let's be honest: the Active Cash and Double Cash both do 2%, so the Quicksilver's 1.5% base rate is the weakest link. On $20,000 in annual spending, that's a $100 difference. Not nothing. But if you book through Capital One Travel, that 5% rate can narrow the gap fast on a single vacation. And internationally, the Quicksilver actually beats 2% cards that charge 3% FTF — math is math.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
Capital One keeps it simple — which is exactly what you want from a cash back card:

  • Statement credit — apply cash back to your balance at any amount. No minimums.
  • Cover a recent purchase — apply your cash back directly to a recent purchase.
  • Check — receive a physical check (old school, but it works).
  • Gift cards — redeem for select retailer gift cards.
  • Amazon purchases — use rewards at checkout on Amazon.com.
  • PayPal — use rewards to pay when you check out with PayPal.

No minimum redemption amount, cash back never expires, and you've got half a dozen ways to use it. Capital One's redemption flexibility is among the best in the industry. No hoops, no games.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
No annual travel credits, no lounge access — this isn't a travel card. But the travel insurance benefits are surprisingly legit for a free card. One catch: the coverage below comes from Capital One's benefits guide for Quicksilver cards on the Discover network. If your card still has a Mastercard or Visa logo, check Capital One's guide for that network instead, because the coverage can differ:

  • Travel accident insurance — coverage when you book travel with the card.
  • Auto rental collision/theft coverage — secondary in the U.S., primary when you rent outside your home country, on rental cars charged to the card. Skip the rental counter upsell and save yourself $15-$30/day.
  • Baggage delay insurance — up to $100/day for 3 days when luggage arrives 4+ hours late.
  • Lost or damaged luggage — up to $3,000 per trip when you put the fare on the card.
  • Trip cancellation/interruption — up to $1,500 per person for non-refundable fares charged to the card.
  • 24-hour travel assistance — emergency card replacement and cash advances if your card is lost or stolen while traveling.
  • No foreign transaction fees — the standout benefit for international travelers. Most no-annual-fee cards charge 3%.

These protections are the kind of thing you don't think about until you need them — and when you do, you'll be glad you had this card in your wallet.

The Quicksilver loses the earning rate battle to the Active Cash and Double Cash — that's just a fact. But it wins decisively on two fronts: no foreign transaction fees (saving you 3% on every international purchase) and a travel insurance package that no other card in this tier matches. If you never leave the country and don't care about insurance, get the Active Cash. If you travel internationally or want built-in protections, the Quicksilver is the smarter pick despite the lower rate.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:
• International travelers who want a no-annual-fee card they can use abroad without getting hit with FTF surcharges.
  • People who value simplicity — one rate on everything, nothing to activate, nothing to remember.
  • Travelers who want free insurance — rental car coverage, purchase protection, and luggage coverage are genuinely valuable and most people don't realize they have them.
  • Capital One ecosystem users who book through Capital One Travel for that juicy 5% back.
  • First-time rewards card holders looking for a clean, simple entry point to cash back.

Not the right card for: earning rate maximizers (the Active Cash's 2% is just better domestically), people who want transfer partners (look at the Double Cash or Freedom Unlimited), or anyone who already has a premium travel card that covers insurance and FTF.

title: Citi Rewards+
scouts_verdict:
The Citi Rewards+ was the quirky underdog of the no-annual-fee card world until Citi retired it in July 2025. The round-up feature sounded like a gimmick until you realized that your $2 gas station snack was earning points at a 5x effective rate. Coffee runs, transit taps, quick convenience store stops — the more micro-purchases you made, the more the round-up feature bent the math in your favor. It was a card that rewarded how you spent, not just what you spent.

The 10% points back on redemptions was the other hidden gem — essentially a 10% discount on your first 100,000 redeemed points each year, and literally no other card offered this. Pair it with a Citi Strata Premier for full-value transfer partner access, and suddenly your ThankYou points are booking JetBlue flights and Singapore Airlines business class.

But let's keep it real: as a standalone card, the earning rates were mediocre. The Autograph does 3x on six categories. The Freedom Unlimited does 3x on dining. The Rewards+ only really sang as part of a Citi card strategy — you used it for small purchases, pooled your ThankYou points, and let the round-ups and 10% back do their thing. On its own, there are better options. As a sidekick, it was genuinely clever. Just know this is a eulogy now: Citi folded every Rewards+ into the Citi Strata in July 2025, and the last holdovers kept the round-ups and 10% back only until July 19, 2026.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Citi Rewards+ Card was one of those cards that sounded gimmicky until you actually ran the numbers. Its trick: round-up rewards that bumped every purchase to the nearest 10 ThankYou points, plus 10% points back on redemptions (the first 100,000 points a year). A $1.50 coffee earned 10 points instead of 1. Redeeming 10,000 points got you 1,000 back. It was like the card had a built-in loyalty bonus on top of your loyalty bonus.

Important note: As of July 2025, all Citi Rewards+ cards have been converted to the Citi Strata Card. If you opened your Rewards+ between July 20, 2024 and July 19, 2025, you kept the round-up and 10% points back features until July 19, 2026 — and that window has now closed, so no former Rewards+ account earns round-ups or the 10% rebate anymore. This page is a look back at how the Rewards+ worked; if you're shopping today, its successor is the Citi Strata Card (3x at supermarkets, gas/EV charging, select transit and one category you pick; 2x at restaurants).

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• Round-up rewards — every purchase rounded up to the nearest 10 ThankYou points. A $3 coffee earned 10 points instead of 3. A $7 lunch earned 10 instead of 7. The smaller and more frequent your purchases, the more this feature shone — until it ended along with the 10% points back.
  • 10% points back when you redeemed ThankYou points, on the first 100,000 points each year (so up to 10,000 points back). It was essentially a 10% discount on everything you redeemed — until Citi retired it along with the card.
  • 2x ThankYou points at U.S. supermarkets and gas stations
  • 1x ThankYou point on all other purchases
  • $0 annual fee — free to hold.
  • Transfer partners at a discount: On its own, the no-fee Strata (what every Rewards+ became) can transfer to most of Citi's airline and hotel partners, but at reduced ratios — most airlines at 10:7, so 1,000 points become 700 miles. Pair with a Strata Premier or Strata Elite to unlock full-value ratios (1:1 on nearly every airline) across all 20 partners — 15 airlines and 5 hotel programs, including American AAdvantage.
  • Citi Entertainment — access to presale tickets and VIP experiences.

No annual fee means it costs nothing to keep in your wallet. The 3% foreign transaction fee is a deal-breaker for international use though — leave this one at home when you travel abroad.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
The Citi Rewards+ previously offered 20,000 bonus ThankYou points after spending $1,500 in purchases within the first 3 months — worth $200 in gift cards or statement credits, or potentially more through transfer partners.

Since the card has transitioned to the Citi Strata, new applicants should look at the Citi Strata Card, which offers a similar 20,000-point welcome bonus with a lower $1,000 spend requirement. Heads up: as of September 2026, Citi's terms say the Strata bonus isn't available if you currently have or previously had a Citi Strata (or Citi Strata Student) account — and since every Rewards+ was converted into a Strata, an old Rewards+ may well count against you. Citi's bonus rules are strict — plan accordingly.

On paper, these rates are nothing special. But the round-up feature was where the magic happened on small purchases. That $3 coffee? 10 points — effectively a 3.3x rate. A $1 pack of gum? Still 10 points — a 10x rate. The more small purchases you made, the more the math tilted in your favor. The card rewarded frequency over transaction size, which made it the perfect companion for a daily coffee habit — until the round-up ended (July 19, 2026 for the last holdover accounts).

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
ThankYou points earned with the Rewards+/Strata can be put to work in a few ways:

  • Statement credits — 1 cent per point. Simple.
  • Gift cards — select retailers at 1 cent per point.
  • Shop with points at Amazon and other participating retailers.
  • Transfer to partners — and this is the big one. When paired with an eligible Citi card (Strata Premier, Strata Elite, or legacy Premier/Prestige), you unlock full-value transfers to partners like JetBlue, Singapore Airlines, Virgin Atlantic, Turkish Airlines, and more. On its own, the no-fee card transfers at a reduced ratio (mostly 10:7).

The 10% points back on redemptions was the card's secret weapon. Redeem 10,000 points, get 1,000 back. Every redemption (on your first 100,000 points a year) was effectively worth 10% more. No other card did this — and after July 19, 2026, not even this one does.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
Let's be upfront: the Rewards+ / Strata base card is not a travel card. No credits, no lounge access, no premium insurance. Here's what you do get:

  • Citi Entertainment — presale access to concerts, sports, dining, and other events. Nice for snagging tickets before the general public.
  • Citi ThankYou travel portal — book flights, hotels, and car rentals at 1 cent per point.
  • Transfer partners (reduced ratios on its own, mostly 10:7; full value when paired with a Strata Premier or Elite) — this is how your ThankYou points become airline miles worth significantly more than 1 cent each.

With a 3% foreign transaction fee and no travel insurance, keep this card domestic. It's built for everyday spending at supermarkets, gas stations, and coffee shops — not for globetrotting. Pair it with a travel card that handles the international stuff.

Here's the honest truth: the Rewards+ earning rates lose to basically every competitor listed here. The Autograph does 3x across six categories with standalone transfer access. The Freedom Unlimited does 3x on dining and drugstores. The SavorOne does 3x on dining, entertainment, and groceries. Where the Rewards+ carved out its niche was the round-up trick and the 10% points back — features nobody else offered, and both are now gone for good. They worked best as accelerators within a Citi card strategy, not as your only card.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:
Back when it was open (and before the round-ups and 10% back ended), the Rewards+ was best for:

  • Frequent small-purchase buyers — if your day involves coffee, transit taps, convenience store runs, and quick bites, the round-up feature turned micro-purchases into surprisingly efficient point earners.
  • Citi ecosystem builders who already have (or plan to get) a Strata Premier or Elite for full-value transfer partner access. The Rewards+ was the perfect wingman card.
  • Grocery and gas spenders who want 2x at supermarkets and gas stations without paying an annual fee.
  • Points poolers who want to combine ThankYou points across multiple Citi cards for bigger redemptions.

Not the right fit for: people who want strong earning rates across many categories (the Autograph's 3x on six categories is objectively better), international travelers (3% FTF is a non-starter), or anyone who doesn't want to pair this with a premium Citi card to unlock full-value transfers. As a solo card, there are stronger options. As part of a Citi strategy, it was a clever little earner.

title: Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business
scouts_verdict:
Look, $795 is a lot of money. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But Chase built the Sapphire Reserve for Business for a specific kind of business owner — one who travels regularly, runs digital ads, and actually uses premium perks — and for that person, the math is borderline absurd.

Between the $300 travel credit, $500 in Edit hotel credits, Google Workspace and ZipRecruiter credits, and the gift card perk, you're looking at $1,500+ in tangible credits before you even count lounge access or points earning. The 3x on advertising spend is a genuine differentiator that no other premium travel card matches, and 8x on everything in Chase Travel is one of the richest portal earning rates in the business card space.

My take: if your business spends at least $50K/year on the card and you travel six or more times annually, this card pays for itself and then some. The Sapphire Lounges are legitimately great, the Ultimate Rewards ecosystem is best-in-class, and the Flex option gives you a safety valve when cash flow gets bumpy. If that doesn't describe your business, the Capital One Venture X Business gives you 80% of the experience at half the price. But for high-spending, high-traveling businesses? The Reserve for Business is the one to beat.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business is Chase's premium business travel card, and it's a big swing. At $795 per year, it's one of the priciest mainstream business cards on the market (the $895 Amex Business Platinum costs even more). But here's the thing — Chase packed it with so much value that it can actually deliver over $2,500 in annual benefits if you use everything.

Launched in mid-2025, this card is built for business owners who travel regularly and want a single card that covers flights, hotels, lounges, and even business software credits. It's technically a pay-in-full charge card, but Chase built in a Flex for Business option that lets you revolve a portion of your balance if needed. Think of it as a hybrid — the discipline of a charge card with the flexibility of a credit card when cash flow gets tight.

The earning structure is aggressive: 8x on Chase Travel, 4x on direct airline and hotel bookings, and 3x on social media and search advertising — a category few cards reward, and no other premium travel card does. If your business runs Meta ads or Google campaigns, that 3x alone can be worth hundreds of dollars a year.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• $300 Annual Travel Credit — Automatically applies to a broad range of travel purchases including parking, tolls, and transit. No hoops to jump through.
  • $500 Annual Credit for The Edit — Up to $250 per transaction on Chase's curated hotel booking platform, up to $500 per calendar year on prepaid stays of two nights or more. Chase doubles it to $1,000 a year starting 1/1/2027.
  • Chase Sapphire Lounge + Priority Pass — Access to Chase's own premium lounges plus 1,300+ Priority Pass lounges worldwide, each with two complimentary guests.
  • IHG One Rewards Platinum Elite Status — Complimentary through 12/31/2027. Gets you room upgrades, late checkout, and bonus points at IHG properties.
  • $200 Google Workspace Credit — Annual statement credit on Google Workspace purchases.
  • Up to $400 ZipRecruiter Credit — $200 per half-year on ZipRecruiter, handy if you're actively hiring.
  • $120 Global Entry/TSA PreCheck Credit — Covers the application fee every four years.
  • $100 Annual Gift Card Credit — $50 per half-year on gift card purchases.
  • 5x on Lyft — Through 9/30/2027, plus a $10 monthly Lyft credit.
  • Up to 99 Employee Cards — At no additional cost, all earning points on the same account.
  • No Foreign Transaction Fees — Use it internationally without the typical 3% surcharge.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
The annual fee is $795 — no getting around it, that's steep. But the $300 travel credit kicks in automatically, effectively reducing your net fee to $495 before you even think about the other perks.

If you layer in The Edit credits ($500), the Google Workspace credit ($200), ZipRecruiter credits ($400), and the gift card credit ($100), the total credits alone add up to $1,500. That means the card can pay for itself nearly twice over if your business actually uses these services.

There are no foreign transaction fees and no fees for employee cards (up to 99). The pay-in-full structure means no interest charges on your main balance, though the Flex for Business revolving option will carry a variable APR if you use it.

Bottom line: $795 is a lot. But if your business travels and advertises online, the math works. If you're a solo freelancer who flies twice a year, look elsewhere.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
The current welcome offer is 200,000 bonus Ultimate Rewards points after spending $30,000 on purchases in your first 6 months. Chase pegs that at $4,000 if you redeem through Points Boost on select Chase Travel flights and hotels (2 cents a point); as cash or a regular Chase Travel booking it's $2,000. Heads up: Chase says the bonus may not be available if you've ever had this card.

That $30,000 spend requirement is significant, but with six months to hit it, it's realistic for a business card — if you're running payroll, buying inventory, or paying for advertising, you can hit it without forcing extra purchases.

For context, the card launched in 2025 with this same blockbuster 200,000-point offer, dropped to 150,000 for a while, and Chase has now brought the 200,000 back. It's one of the richest welcome bonuses in the business card space. Combined with the points you'd earn on that $30,000 in spending, you're looking at 230,000+ total points in your first six months.

sections.title: Earning Rates
sections.content:
This is where the Sapphire Reserve for Business really flexes:

  • 8x points on all Chase Travel purchases — flights, hotels (including The Edit), car rentals, cruises, activities, and tours booked through the Chase Travel portal.
  • 5x total points on Lyft — Through September 30, 2027.
  • 4x points on flights and hotels booked directly with airlines and hotel chains.
  • 3x points on social media and search engine advertising — think Google Ads, Meta Ads, LinkedIn Ads. This is a huge deal for businesses running digital campaigns. Starting 11/15/2026, the 3x covers the first $1 million in ad spend each account anniversary year (1x after that), a cap very few businesses will hit.
  • 1x point on everything else.

The 8x on Chase Travel is eye-catching, and it's genuinely useful if you book through their portal. But even at 4x on direct bookings, you're earning at a rate that matches or beats most competitors. The 3x on advertising spend stands out — no other premium travel card offers a bonus category on ad spend, which is often one of the biggest line items for small businesses.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
Ultimate Rewards points are among the most versatile rewards currencies out there. Here's how you can use them:

  • Chase Travel Portal — Points are worth 1 cent each on regular Chase Travel bookings, but Points Boost deals on select flights and hotels can push them up to 2 cents each.
  • Transfer Partners — Transfer 1:1 to Chase's airline and hotel partners, including United, Hyatt, Southwest, British Airways, Air France/KLM, Singapore Airlines, and more. This is where you can extract outsized value — transferring to Hyatt alone can get you 2-4 cents per point.
  • Cash Back — Redeem at 1 cent per point as a statement credit or direct deposit (same as a regular Chase Travel booking, but well short of what transfers can get).
  • Gift Cards & Shopping — Available but generally not the best value.

The sweet spot is transfer partners. A single Hyatt redemption at a top-tier property can make those 200,000 bonus points worth $5,000+. Just don't count on a guaranteed portal floor: outside of Points Boost deals, Chase Travel redemptions are 1 cent a point, same as cash.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
The travel perks on this card are stacked. Let's break them all down:

  • $300 Annual Travel Credit — Applies broadly to travel purchases including airfare, hotels, car rentals, parking, tolls, and transit. This is one of the easiest credits to use — no portal required, no specific merchants.
  • $500 Annual Credit for The Edit — Chase's handpicked collection of hotels and resorts. Up to $500 per calendar year, with a $250 max per transaction and a two-night minimum prepaid stay, and it doubles to $1,000 a year starting 1/1/2027. Edit stays also come with perks like a $100 property credit and daily breakfast for two.
  • $250 Select Hotel Credit — For prepaid Chase Travel hotel bookings (two-night minimum) through 12/31/2026 at select chains: IHG, Montage, Pendry, Omni, Virgin Hotels, Minor Hotels, and Pan Pacific.
  • Chase Sapphire Lounge Access — Chase's own premium lounge network, which is genuinely impressive — think craft cocktails, chef-driven menus, and shower suites. Two complimentary guests included.
  • Priority Pass Select — Access to 1,300+ lounges worldwide with two complimentary guests. Solid fallback when there's no Sapphire Lounge at your airport.
  • IHG One Rewards Platinum Elite — Room upgrades when available, late checkout, welcome amenity, and bonus points. Valid through 12/31/2027.
  • Global Entry / TSA PreCheck / NEXUS — Up to $120 credit every four years.
  • $10 Monthly Lyft Credit — Nice for airport rides.

Between the travel credit, The Edit credit, and lounge access alone, you're looking at over $1,600 in annual travel value. That more than covers the $795 fee if you actually use these perks.

sections.content:
The premium business card space has three serious contenders. Here's how they stack up:

The verdict: The Amex Business Platinum wins on lounge access (Centurion Lounges are still the gold standard) and has the broadest transfer partner network. But its airline credit is annoyingly restrictive, it costs $100 more, and it lacks a bonus category for advertising spend. The Capital One Venture X Business is the value play at $395/year — simpler benefits, solid earning rates, and Capital One's own lounges are excellent. The Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business sits in the middle on price ($100 less than the Amex, $400 more than Capital One), with the best earning rates for businesses that book travel and run digital ads. If your business spends heavily on advertising and travel, Chase wins. If you want simplicity and lower cost, go Capital One.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:
• Business owners who travel frequently — The 8x on Chase Travel, lounge access, and travel credits make this a no-brainer for road warriors.
  • Companies running digital advertising — That 3x on social media and search ads is rare for a premium travel card. If you spend $5,000/month on Google or Meta ads, that's 180,000 points per year.
  • Teams that need employee cards — Up to 99 free employee cards, all earning points on the main account.
  • Businesses already in the Chase ecosystem — If you have a Chase Ink card or bank with Chase, the points pool together and the relationship benefits compound.
  • Entrepreneurs who value premium perks — Sapphire Lounges, IHG Platinum status, and The Edit hotel credits appeal to business travelers who want comfort, not just points.

This card is not ideal for solo freelancers with minimal travel, businesses with tight margins that can't justify $795, or anyone who won't use the credits and perks. The value equation depends entirely on activation — if you ignore the credits, you're just paying a very expensive annual fee for 1x earning on most purchases.

title: Capital One Venture X Business
scouts_verdict:
The Capital One Venture X Business is the rare premium card that doesn't require mental gymnastics to justify keeping. At $395 with a $300 travel credit and 10K anniversary miles, you're essentially getting paid to carry it — and that's before you earn a single mile on purchases.

The 2X flat rate everywhere is genuinely best-in-class for a premium business card, the transfer partners are strong enough for aspirational redemptions, and the lounge access (especially the Capital One Lounges) adds real quality-of-life value for road warriors. The charge card structure with no preset spending limit is the cherry on top for businesses that need flexibility.

Is it perfect? No. The $30K welcome bonus spend requirement is steep, the portal-only bonus categories limit earning for those who book direct, and the transfer partner list — while solid — still lacks some Amex Membership Rewards heavy hitters like ANA, Delta, Hilton and Marriott. But for the price? Nothing in the premium business card space comes close to this value proposition. Scout's Rating: 9.2/10

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Venture X Business is basically the personal Venture X's cooler older sibling — same DNA, but with a business expense report. It's a charge card, not a traditional credit card, which means it's designed to be paid in full each month (you can carry over a portion of the balance, but at a steep variable APR) and there's no preset spending limit. That last part is huge for businesses with lumpy or seasonal expenses.

For $395 a year, you get a travel rewards card that practically pays for itself before you even start swiping. Between the $300 annual travel credit and 10,000 anniversary miles (worth ~$100), the effective cost drops to something laughably low for a premium card. Capital One has essentially built the value equation that made the personal Venture X a smash hit, then turbocharged it with business-friendly features like employee card controls and expense management tools.

The card earns Capital One miles, which transfer (mostly 1:1) to 20+ airline and hotel partners — the same pool you'd access with the personal Venture X. That means access to sweet spots like Air Canada Aeroplan, Turkish Miles & Smiles, and Virgin Red for outsized redemption value.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• $300 annual Capital One Business Travel credit — automatically applied to bookings through Capital One Business Travel
  • 10,000 bonus miles every anniversary — worth roughly $100 in travel, further offsetting the annual fee
  • Lounge access — Capital One Lounges, Priority Pass (1,300+ lounges worldwide), plus 2 free guests at Priority Pass lounges
  • No preset spending limit — adapts to your business spending patterns over time
  • $100 experience credit for Capital One Premier Collection hotel bookings
  • Up to $120 Global Entry / TSA PreCheck credit
  • No foreign transaction fees
  • Employee cards at no extra cost — with customizable spending limits and real-time transaction tracking
  • Cell phone protection — up to $800 per claim when you pay your monthly bill with the card
  • Travel protections — trip cancellation/interruption insurance, travel accident insurance, auto rental collision damage waiver

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
The annual fee is $395. But here's the thing — this is one of those cards where the "effective" annual fee is what actually matters.

  • $300 travel credit knocks it down to $95
  • 10,000 anniversary miles (~$100 value) make it essentially free, or even net positive

Since this is a charge card, it's designed to be paid in full each month. Capital One does let you carry over a portion of your balance if you really need to, but that portion gets hit with a variable APR (25.74% as of September 2026), and missing the minimum payment triggers a 2.99% late fee. Treat the carry-over option as an emergency valve, not a financing plan — pay in full and those 2X miles stay pure profit.

There are no foreign transaction fees, which is table stakes for a premium travel card but still worth mentioning. Employee cards are free, though if you want them to have their own lounge access, that's an extra $125/year per additional cardholder (as of February 2026).

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
The current welcome offer is 150,000 miles after spending $30,000 in the first 3 months. That $30K spend requirement is hefty — this is clearly aimed at businesses with real expenses, not someone putting a few dinners on a card.

Those 150,000 miles are worth at least $1,500 when redeemed through the Capital One travel portal at 1 cent per mile, but savvy travelers can squeeze out significantly more through transfer partners. Book business class to Asia through Air Canada Aeroplan or Turkish Miles & Smiles and you could get $3,000–$5,000+ in value from that bonus.

For context, Capital One previously ran a limited-time 400K offer (with a $150K total spend requirement) that ended in early 2026 — so the current 150K offer, while solid, is the standard public bonus. Keep an eye out for elevated offers that pop up periodically.

sections.title: Earning Rates
sections.content:
The earning structure is refreshingly simple, with bonus categories that actually make sense for business travelers:

  • 10X miles on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Business Travel
  • 5X miles on flights and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Business Travel
  • 2X miles on everything else — no caps, no categories to track, no activation required

That flat 2X on everything is the real workhorse here. Office supplies, software subscriptions, client dinners, that emergency printer cartridge — it all earns double miles without you having to think about it. And unlike some competitors that cap their bonus categories, the 10X and 5X portal rates are unlimited too.

The catch? Those elevated rates only apply when booking through Capital One Business Travel, not directly with airlines or hotels. The portal's pricing is generally competitive, but power users who rely on direct bookings for elite status credits should weigh that trade-off.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
Capital One miles are flexible, and the redemption options range from "perfectly fine" to "absurdly valuable" depending on how much effort you want to put in:

  • Transfer to 20+ airline and hotel partners (best value) — most at 1:1 ratios. Top partners include Air Canada Aeroplan, Turkish Miles & Smiles, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Avianca LifeMiles, Singapore KrisFlyer, Virgin Red, and British Airways Avios.
  • Book through Capital One Travel — redeem at 1 cent per mile, simple and straightforward
  • Cover recent travel purchases — erase travel charges from the past 90 days at 1 cent per mile
  • Gift cards — 0.8 cents per mile (meh)
  • Cash back — 0.5 cents per mile (don't do this)

The transfer partner sweet spot is where this card truly shines. You can book Lufthansa First Class, ANA business class, or Singapore Suites through partners for a fraction of the cash price. Hotel transfers go to Accor (2:1 ratio), Choice Privileges (1:1), Wyndham Rewards (1:1), and I Prefer Hotel Rewards (1:2).

One nice perk: there's no minimum redemption for portal bookings, though you need at least 1,000 miles to transfer to partners.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
This is where the Venture X Business really earns its keep:

  • $300 annual travel credit — applied automatically to any booking through Capital One Business Travel. Unlike some competitors' credits that require specific merchants or convoluted workarounds, this one is dead simple. Book a flight, hotel, or rental car through the portal, and the credit applies. It resets every cardmember year.
  • 10,000 anniversary miles — deposited into your account each year on your card anniversary. Worth ~$100 at baseline, more if transferred to partners.
  • $100 experience credit — for bookings at Capital One Premier Collection properties (think boutique and luxury hotels with extra perks like room upgrades and late checkout).
  • Up to $120 Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit — statement credit every 4 years when you use your card to pay the application fee.

Lounge access is a headline perk. You get entry to:

  • Capital One Lounges — currently in Dallas (DFW), Denver (DEN), Washington Dulles (IAD), Las Vegas (LAS), and New York (JFK), plus restaurant-style Capital One Landings at Washington National (DCA) and New York LaGuardia (LGA), with Charlotte (CLT) up next. These are genuinely excellent lounges with craft cocktails, chef-prepared food, and even shower suites. Heads up: guests aren't free here anymore — it's $45 per adult guest unless you spend $75,000 on the card in a calendar year, which unlocks 2 free guests (1 at Landings).
  • Priority Pass — 1,300+ lounges in nearly 150 countries. Primary cardholders can bring 2 guests for free.

Note: Direct Plaza Premium Lounge access was removed in March 2025, though many Plaza Premium locations remain accessible via Priority Pass.

sections.title: Competitor Comparison
sections.content:
Let's see how the Venture X Business stacks up against the other heavy hitters in the premium business travel card space:

FeatureVenture X Business ($395/yr)Amex Business Platinum ($895/yr)Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business ($795/yr)
Welcome Bonus150K miles / $30K spend200K MR / $20K spend (targeted offers up to 300K)200K UR / $30K spend
Base Earning2X everywhere1X (2X on key business categories & $5K+ purchases)1X everywhere
Travel Earning5X–10X via portal5X flights & prepaid hotels via Amex Travel8X via Chase Travel, 4X flights & hotels booked direct
Annual Travel Credit$300 (easy to use)$200 airline fee + up to $600 hotel via Amex Travel (restrictive)$300 travel credit
Lounge AccessCapital One Lounges + Priority PassCenturion Lounges + Priority Pass + Delta Sky Club (10 visits/yr w/ Delta flights)Sapphire Lounges + Priority Pass + select Air Canada Maple Leaf Lounges (w/ Star Alliance flights)
Transfer Partners20+ (mostly 1:1)20 (includes ANA, Delta, Hilton, Marriott)14 (1:1)
Card TypeCharge cardCharge cardCredit card

The verdict: The Venture X Business offers the best value-to-fee ratio of the three. The Amex Business Platinum has a superior lounge network (Centurion Lounges are hard to beat) and some transfer partners Capital One lacks (ANA, Delta, Hilton, Marriott), but at $500 more per year. The Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business charges roughly double the annual fee and its 1X base earn rate outside bonus categories is a real weakness. If you want the most premium perks money can buy, the Amex wins. If you want the smartest bang for your buck, the Venture X Business is the play.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:
• Business owners who travel regularly — the combination of portal earning rates, lounge access, and the $300 travel credit make this a no-brainer for frequent flyers
  • Businesses with high monthly spend — the 2X flat rate on everything means your office rent, payroll software, and supply orders are all quietly generating serious miles
  • Points & miles enthusiasts — access to Capital One's 20+ transfer partners means you can punch way above your weight on business class and first class redemptions
  • Business owners who want simplicity — unlike the Amex Platinum with its maze of credits and enrolled benefits, the Venture X Business is refreshingly straightforward: spend, earn 2X, use your credits, done
  • Companies that need flexible spending capacity — the no preset spending limit charge card structure adapts as your business grows

Who should skip it: If your business spends under $30K in 3 months, the welcome bonus will be hard to hit. If you never travel and just want cash back, look elsewhere. And if you specifically need Centurion Lounge access or Delta SkyClub perks, the Amex Business Platinum remains the move.

title: World of Hyatt Credit Card
scouts_verdict: The World of Hyatt card is the best hotel credit card in the game, full stop. At $95 per year, you get a free night certificate worth $150-$300+, a path to a second free night, automatic Discoverist status, and access to one of the few hotel loyalty programs where points are still genuinely valuable. Pair it with a Chase Ultimate Rewards card that transfers to Hyatt (the Sapphire Reserve still goes 1:1) and you've got a hotel rewards machine that punches way above its weight class. If you stay at Hyatt even occasionally, get this card.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The World of Hyatt Credit Card is, in my not-so-humble opinion, the single best hotel credit card in existence. At $95 per year, it gives you access to one of the most valuable hotel loyalty programs in the game — where points regularly deliver 2+ cents in value and free nights at properties that would cost $300-$500 per night. That's not hype. That's math.

You earn World of Hyatt points, which are uniquely valuable because Hyatt still sticks to a published award chart (even after its May 2026 price increases), while Marriott and Hilton have scrapped theirs for dynamic pricing. A Category 1-4 free night certificate (which you get every anniversary) can easily be worth $150-$300 depending on the property. And because you can also earn these points via Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers from cards like the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve, you're plugged into the entire Chase ecosystem.

If you stay at Hyatt even a few times a year — or you're willing to try — this card pays for itself almost immediately. The free night alone covers the fee. Everything else is gravy.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• Free Night Award (Category 1-4): One free night at any Category 1-4 Hyatt property every cardmember anniversary. This alone can be worth $150-$300+ and more than covers the $95 annual fee.
  • Bonus Free Night at $15K Spend: Spend $15,000 in a calendar year and earn an additional free night at any Category 1-4 property. Two free nights per year for a $95 card is absurd value.
  • Automatic Discoverist Status: Complimentary World of Hyatt Discoverist elite status, which gets you late checkout (when available), premium Wi-Fi, and a 10% bonus on base points earned.
  • 5 Qualifying Night Credits Annually + 2 per $5K Spend: Receive 5 qualifying night credits each calendar year, plus earn 2 additional qualifying night credits for every $5,000 you spend. This is a realistic path to Hyatt's top-tier status for big spenders.
  • No Foreign Transaction Fees: Use it internationally without the 3% surcharge. Essential for Hyatt stays abroad.
  • Chase Ultimate Rewards Integration: Chase UR points transfer to Hyatt 1:1 through the Sapphire Reserve, and you can pool points from Freedom Flex, Freedom Unlimited and Ink cards there first. Heads up: the Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred now transfer at a weaker 4:3 (1,000 UR = 750 Hyatt points) — right away for Sapphire Preferred cardholders who applied on or after June 15, 2026, and for everyone else from October 1, 2026. Still the real superpower.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
• Annual Fee: $95 — a steal for what you get. The free night certificate alone is worth more.
  • Authorized User Fee: $0. Add your partner and earn points faster.
  • Foreign Transaction Fees: None
  • APR: 19.24% - 27.74% variable, based on creditworthiness
  • Balance Transfer Fee: 5% of the amount transferred, $5 minimum
  • Late Payment Fee: Up to $40

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn 30,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening, plus up to 30,000 additional bonus points by earning 2x on purchases that normally earn 1x in the first 6 months (on up to $15,000 in spending).

That's a potential 60,000 total bonus points if you max it out — enough for multiple free nights at mid-tier Hyatt properties or one spectacular night at a top-tier resort. At 2+ cents per point, you're looking at $1,200+ in value from a card with a $95 annual fee. The spend requirement is reasonable, and the bonus structure rewards you for actually using the card.

sections.title: Earning Rates
sections.content:
• 9x total points at Hyatt: 4x as a cardholder + 5x as a World of Hyatt member on eligible purchases at Hyatt properties. It's not the biggest multiplier out there (the Hilton Aspire earns 14x and the IHG Premier 10x on the card alone), but Hyatt points are worth far more apiece, so the return still stacks up.
  • 2x points on: Airline tickets purchased directly from airlines, restaurants, local transit and commuting, and fitness club/gym memberships.
  • 1x points on: Everything else.

The 2x categories are solid and cover everyday spending well. The 1x everywhere else is unremarkable, but that's what a Freedom Unlimited (1.5x) is for — earn UR points there, move them to a Sapphire Reserve and transfer them to Hyatt 1:1. Through a Sapphire Preferred the Hyatt ratio is 4:3 (for all cardholders from October 1, 2026), which trims that 1.5x to about 1.1 Hyatt points per dollar.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
World of Hyatt points can only be redeemed through the Hyatt program — there's no travel portal or cashback option. But honestly, that's fine because Hyatt redemptions are where these points shine.

  • Free Night Awards: 3,000 to 75,000 points per night for a standard room, depending on category and one of five date-based pricing levels (new as of May 20, 2026). Category 1-4 properties (3,000-25,000 points) are the sweet spot.
  • Suite Upgrades: Use points to upgrade qualifying paid stays — 6,000 points per night for a standard suite, confirmed when you book (or by calling Hyatt for an existing reservation).
  • Experiences: Redeem for unique Hyatt experiences and events.
  • Points + Cash: Combine points with cash for stays when you don't have enough for a full award.

The key advantage: even after the May 2026 overhaul (five pricing levels, with top prices up as much as 67%), Hyatt still publishes an award chart, while Marriott and Hilton have gone fully dynamic. A Category 4 night at the Low level (15,000 points) can easily deliver $300+ in value. That's 2 cents per point or better.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
• Anniversary Free Night (Cat 1-4): Worth $150-$300+. This is the card's crown jewel and the primary reason to hold it year after year.
  • Spend Bonus Free Night (Cat 1-4): Hit $15,000 in calendar-year spending and get a second free night certificate. Between both certificates, you're looking at $300-$600+ in annual hotel value.
  • Discoverist Status Perks: 2pm late checkout when available, premium Wi-Fi, and 10% bonus points.
  • Elite Night Credits: 5 qualifying night credits annually, plus 2 additional qualifying nights per $5,000 spent. Spend $50,000 and that's 25 nights toward Globalist's 60 (20 from spend plus the 5 freebies) — combine with actual stays and you have a realistic path to Hyatt's top status.

No statement credits to deal with, no hoops to jump through. Just straightforward free nights and status benefits. Refreshingly simple.

sections.title: Competitor Comparison
sections.content:
• vs. Marriott Bonvoy Boundless ($95/yr): Same annual fee, but Marriott points are worth roughly 0.7-0.8 cents each vs. Hyatt's 2+ cents. The Boundless gives you a 35,000-point free night certificate — which books a mediocre room. Hyatt's Category 1-4 cert books legitimately nice properties. Hyatt wins decisively.
  • vs. Hilton Honors Aspire ($550/yr): The Aspire offers an annual Free Night Reward with no category cap, but at $550/yr with Hilton's notoriously inflated award pricing. You need to extract serious value from the Diamond status and credits to justify it. The Hyatt card does more for less.
  • vs. IHG One Rewards Premier ($99/yr): Similar price point, but IHG points are worth about 0.5 cents each. IHG's fourth-night-free perk is nice for longer stays, but for pure value per point, Hyatt crushes it.
  • vs. Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant ($650/yr): The Brilliant offers an 85,000-point free night and $300 dining credit, but at $650/yr you need to do serious math. The Hyatt card delivers comparable value at $95.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:
• Hyatt loyalists: If you stay at Hyatt even 2-3 times a year, this card is a no-brainer.
  • Chase ecosystem builders: Pair with Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve to transfer UR points to Hyatt for outsized value (the Reserve still goes 1:1; the Preferred drops to 4:3 for all cardholders on October 1, 2026).
  • Value maximizers: If you want the most hotel value per dollar of annual fee, this is it. Period.
  • Status seekers: The 5 qualifying night credits you get each year, plus 2 more per $5,000 spent, chip away at Globalist's 60-night requirement — $50,000 of spend earns 20, so with the annual 5 you're at 25.

Not ideal for: People who don't care about Hyatt specifically, or those who prefer flexible cashback. The points are locked to the Hyatt ecosystem — powerful within it, useless outside it.

title: World of Hyatt Business Credit Card
scouts_verdict: The Hyatt Business card is the power move for business owners who are serious about Hyatt. At $199 (effectively $99 after credits), you get a 70K welcome bonus, automatic 2x on your top spending categories, and a fast track to Globalist status (no free night certificate, though — that's a personal-card perk). Pair it with the personal Hyatt card and you're running a two-card system that generates absurd hotel value. The $7K spend requirement for the bonus is steep for individuals but routine for businesses. If Hyatt is your brand, this is your business card.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card is the big sibling to the personal Hyatt card — and it's built for business owners who want to accelerate their way to Hyatt elite status while earning serious points on everyday business spending. At $199 per year, it costs more than the personal card, but the earning structure and benefits justify the premium if you're putting real business spend on it.

The standout feature is the automatic 2x earning on your top three spending categories each quarter. Chase tracks where your money goes and automatically applies bonus earnings — no activation required, no rotating categories to remember. For businesses with concentrated spending in a few areas, this is quietly powerful.

Combine this with the personal World of Hyatt card and you've got a two-card Hyatt strategy that can generate a mountain of points and elite qualifying nights. If Hyatt is your hotel brand, this is the business card to carry.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• 10% Points Back for Big Spenders: Spend $50,000 in a calendar year and get 10% of your redeemed points back for the rest of that year (on up to 200,000 points redeemed). Note there's no anniversary free night on this card — that perk is personal-card only.
  • $100 Hyatt Statement Credit: Earn up to $100 in statement credits each anniversary year when you spend $50+ at Hyatt properties (two $50 credits). Effectively reduces your net annual fee to $99.
  • Automatic Discoverist Status: World of Hyatt Discoverist status for as long as your account is open — no stays required (Chase says to allow up to 8 weeks after account opening for it to post). You can also gift Discoverist status to up to five employees.
  • 5 Qualifying Nights per $10K Spend: Earn 5 elite qualifying nights toward Globalist for every $10,000 in spending. A clear path to top-tier status through business spend.
  • Free Employee Cards: Add employee cards at no extra cost — all spending earns you points.
  • No Foreign Transaction Fees: Use it for international business travel without surcharges.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
• Annual Fee: $199 — effectively $99 after the $100 Hyatt statement credit.
  • Employee Card Fee: $0. Free employee cards means more points flowing your way.
  • Foreign Transaction Fees: None
  • APR: Variable, 19.24% - 27.74%
  • Late Payment Fee: Up to $40

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn 70,000 bonus points after spending $7,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. Not available if you currently have this card or earned its new-cardmember bonus in the last 24 months.

That's a hefty spend requirement — $7,000 in 3 months — but for a business card, that's often just normal operating expenses. At 1.65-2 cents per point, 70,000 Hyatt points are worth roughly $1,150-$1,400 in hotel stays. You could book up to 5 nights at solid Category 4 properties or 1-2 nights at luxury Category 7 resorts. For a $199 annual fee card, that's an excellent return.

sections.title: Earning Rates
sections.content:
• 9x total points at Hyatt: 4x as a cardholder + 5x as a World of Hyatt member on eligible Hyatt purchases.
  • 2x points on top 3 categories: Automatically earns 2x on your three highest-spending categories each quarter from a list of eight: dining, shipping, airline tickets bought directly from the airline, local transit and commuting, social media and search engine advertising, car rental agencies, gas stations, and internet, cable and phone services. No enrollment needed — Chase figures it out for you.
  • 2x points on: Fitness club and gym memberships.
  • 1x points on: Everything else.

The automatic 2x on top categories is the real differentiator from the personal card. If your business has concentrated spending — say, advertising, shipping, and gas — you're earning 2x on all of it without thinking about it. That's a meaningful upgrade over 1x base earning.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
Same redemption options as the personal card — points go into your World of Hyatt account and can be used for:

  • Free Night Awards: 3,000 to 75,000 points per night for standard rooms, depending on category and demand tier (Hyatt moved to a five-tier chart in May 2026).
  • Suite Upgrades: Confirm suite upgrades with points.
  • Points + Cash: Combine points and cash when you're short.
  • Experiences: Unique Hyatt experiences and events.

Points from both the personal and business cards pool together in your Hyatt account, so there's a real synergy in holding both. More points, more free nights, more status.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
• Complimentary DashPass: 12 months of DashPass when you activate by 12/31/2027, plus $10 off one non-restaurant DoorDash order each quarter through 12/31/2027 while enrolled. (No anniversary free night here — that's the personal card.)
  • $100 Hyatt Credit: Two $50 statement credits when you spend $50+ at Hyatt. Easy to trigger if you stay at Hyatt at all.
  • Discoverist Status: Automatic for as long as your account is open (allow up to 8 weeks to post) — late checkout, premium Wi-Fi, 10% bonus points.
  • Elite Night Acceleration: 5 qualifying nights per $10,000 spent. Combined with the personal card's 5 automatic nights a year plus 2 per $5,000, you can stack qualifying nights fast.
  • 10% Award Redemption Bonus: Spend $50,000 in a calendar year and get 10% of your redeemed points back for the rest of that year (on up to 200,000 points redeemed).

sections.title: Competitor Comparison
sections.content:
• vs. World of Hyatt Personal ($95/yr): The business card costs $104 more on paper (about $4 more after the $100 Hyatt credit) and adds the automatic 2x on top categories and a bigger 70K welcome bonus (vs. up to 60K on the personal card) — but it has no anniversary free night, which the personal card does. If you have real business spend, the business card is worth the upgrade.
  • vs. Chase Ink Business Preferred ($95/yr): The Ink earns 3x on travel, shipping, internet, and advertising — better in those specific categories. But its points are UR, which transfer to Hyatt at 1:1 only through September 30, 2026 — starting October 1, Ink Business Preferred transfers to Hyatt drop to 4:3 (1,000 UR points become 750 Hyatt points), so that 3x works out to 2.25 Hyatt points per dollar. The Hyatt Biz card is better if you want the Hyatt credits, elite-night earning and other Hyatt-specific perks.
  • vs. Marriott Bonvoy Boundless ($95/yr): Lower annual fee but Marriott points are worth less than half what Hyatt points are worth. The Hyatt Biz card delivers more value despite costing more.
  • vs. Capital One Venture X Business ($395/yr): Venture X Business is a premium all-around business card with lounge access. Different use case — the Hyatt Biz is specifically for hotel value maximizers.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:
• Business owners who stay at Hyatt: The combination of points earning, Hyatt credits, and elite status acceleration makes this ideal for Hyatt-loyal business travelers.
  • High-spend businesses: The automatic 2x on top categories rewards concentrated business spending without any category management.
  • Two-card Hyatt strategists: Pair with the personal Hyatt card for maximum points plus the personal card's anniversary free night (the business card doesn't come with one).
  • Status chasers: The qualifying night credits from spending create a viable path to Globalist through business expenses.

Not ideal for: Businesses with low annual spend (the personal card at $95 is better), or those who prefer flexible rewards over hotel-specific points.

title: Southwest Rapid Rewards Plus
scouts_verdict: The Southwest Plus is the budget entry into the Southwest ecosystem. At $99, you're really paying for free checked bags and the 10,000-point Companion Pass boost — and honestly, that's enough for casual Southwest flyers. The earning rates are mediocre and the anniversary points are modest, but if you just need the basics and fly Southwest a few times a year, it does the job. Families especially will love the bag savings. Just know that for $50-$130 more, the Premier and Priority cards offer meaningfully better perks.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Southwest Rapid Rewards Plus is the entry-level Southwest credit card, and at $99 per year it's designed for casual Southwest flyers who want the core perks — free checked bags, some bonus points, and a shot at the legendary Companion Pass — without paying Priority-card prices.

Let's be real: this card exists because Southwest's bag policy changed. Once upon a time, everyone got free bags on Southwest. Now, having a Southwest credit card is the easiest way to keep that perk alive. The Plus card is the cheapest way in, and for many flyers, that's the only reason they need.

The earning rates are modest (2x on Southwest, 2x on gas and groceries up to $5K, 1x elsewhere), and the 3,000 anniversary points won't blow anyone's mind. But combined with the 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points boost, free bags for your whole group, and the ability to earn toward the Companion Pass, this card delivers solid baseline value for loyal Southwest travelers.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• Free Checked Bags: Cardmember and up to 8 passengers on the same reservation get their first checked bag free. At $45 each way per bag, this adds up fast for families.
  • 10,000 Companion Pass Qualifying Points: Automatic annual boost toward the Companion Pass — the most valuable perk in domestic travel.
  • 3,000 Anniversary Points: Not huge, but worth about $39-$45 toward Southwest flights. Offsets part of the annual fee.
  • 25% Back on Inflight Purchases: Statement credit of 25% when you pay for inflight drinks with your Southwest card. (Wi-Fi is already free for Rapid Rewards members.)
  • Standard Seat Selection: Complimentary Standard seat within 48 hours of departure (when available).
  • 10% Annual Flight Discount: Promo code for 10% off Southwest flights every cardmember anniversary (excludes Basic fares).
  • Group 5 Boarding: Cardmember and up to 8 passengers board in Group 5.
  • No Foreign Transaction Fees: Southwest flies to Mexico and the Caribbean too, so this comes in handy for spending on those trips or anywhere else abroad.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
• Annual Fee: $99 — the cheapest Southwest card option.
  • Foreign Transaction Fees: None
  • APR: Variable, typically 19.24% - 27.74%
  • Balance Transfer Fee: 5% of the amount transferred, $5 minimum
  • Late Payment Fee: Up to $40

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
The standard offer is 50,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months. That's a very low spend requirement — about $333/month — making this one of the easiest airline card bonuses to earn. One catch: it's off-limits if you currently have a personal Southwest card or earned a bonus on one in the past 24 months.

50,000 Rapid Rewards points can get you 2-4 round-trip domestic flights depending on routes and timing. At roughly 1.3 cents per point, that's about $650 in Southwest flight value from a card with a $99 annual fee.

Periodically, Southwest runs limited-time offers that include Companion Pass — which is wildly more valuable. If you see a Companion Pass offer, jump on it.

sections.title: Earning Rates
sections.content:
• 2x points on: Southwest Airlines purchases.
  • 2x points on: Gas stations and grocery stores (on the first $5,000 in combined purchases per year, then 1x).
  • 1x points on: Everything else.

The earning rates are... fine. Not exciting. The $5,000 cap on gas and grocery bonus earnings is restrictive — that's only about $417/month before you drop to 1x. If you're a heavier spender, the Premier or Priority cards offer better earning potential.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
Southwest Rapid Rewards points redeem directly for Southwest flights with no blackout dates, no award charts, and no seat restrictions. The value fluctuates based on the cash price of the flight.

  • Southwest Flights: Points cover the fare (you still pay taxes/fees in cash). Typical value is 1.2-1.5 cents per point.
  • Cash + Points: Short on points? Pay for a flight with a mix of cash and points.
  • Hotel & Car Rentals: Redeemable through Southwest's More Rewards program, though values are generally worse than flights.
  • Gift Cards & Merchandise: Available but poor value — stick to flights.

The simplicity is Southwest's strength. No complicated award charts, no devaluation anxiety. The price you see is the price you pay in points.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
• Free Checked Bags: The headline perk. At $45 per bag each way, a family of four saves $360 per round trip.
  • 25% Inflight Credit: Get 25% back on inflight drinks bought with your Southwest card (Wi-Fi is already free for Rapid Rewards members).
  • 3,000 Anniversary Points: Worth ~$39-$45 in flight value. Modest but consistent.
  • 10,000 Companion Pass QP Boost: Automatic head start toward the 135,000 qualifying points needed for the Companion Pass.
  • Standard Seat Pick: Choose a Standard seat within 48 hours of departure. Want a Preferred seat at booking or free Extra Legroom upgrades? That's the Priority card.

The Plus card is stripped-down compared to its siblings. No free Preferred seat, no Extra Legroom upgrades, no A-List tier points from spending, fewer anniversary points. You're paying for the bag benefit and the Companion Pass qualifying points — and for many people, that's enough.

sections.title: Competitor Comparison
sections.content:
• vs. Southwest Premier ($149/yr): For $50 more, you get 3x on Southwest (vs 2x), 2x on groceries and restaurants on up to $8,000 a year (the Plus's 2x covers gas and groceries up to $5,000), a free Preferred seat within 48 hours of departure, 6,000 anniversary points, and a 15% promo code (vs the Plus's 10%). If you fly Southwest more than a few times a year, the Premier is worth the upgrade.
  • vs. Southwest Priority ($229/yr): The full-featured option with 7,500 anniversary points, 4x on Southwest, uncapped 2x on gas and restaurants, a Preferred seat at booking, and free Extra Legroom upgrades within 48 hours of departure. Best for frequent Southwest flyers.
  • vs. Chase Sapphire Preferred ($95/yr): If you don't fly Southwest often, the CSP offers transferable points to 14+ partners (including Southwest) with better everyday earning rates. More flexible overall.
  • vs. Delta SkyMiles Gold ($150/yr): An even richer bag benefit for Delta flyers: first checked bag free on Delta flights, plus a second free bag on domestic Delta flights. The right pick depends on which airline you fly — loyalty to the airline matters more than card-to-card comparison here.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:
• Casual Southwest flyers: If you fly Southwest 2-4 times a year and want free bags without paying Priority prices.
  • Families on a budget: The free checked bag benefit for up to 8 companions is huge for family travel.
  • Companion Pass chasers: The 10,000 QP annual boost gives you a running start, and the welcome bonus can get you even closer.
  • Minimalists: You want one Southwest card for the basics and don't need premium perks.

Not ideal for: Frequent Southwest flyers (upgrade to Premier or Priority), heavy spenders (the earning rates and caps are too limiting), or travelers who want flexible points (get a Sapphire Preferred instead).

title: Southwest Rapid Rewards Priority
scouts_verdict: The Southwest Priority lost some shine when the $75 travel credit disappeared at the end of 2025, and the effective annual cost went from ~$57 to ~$132. But the new assigned-seating perks — free seat selection at booking and unlimited Extra Legroom upgrades — fill a real gap now that Southwest has ditched open seating. If you fly Southwest 5+ times a year, the combination of seat perks, 7,500 anniversary points, 4x earning, and Group 5 boarding still makes this the right Southwest card. The math just requires a bit more flying to break even than it used to. If you only fly Southwest a couple of times a year, downgrade to the Plus and save yourself $130.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Southwest Rapid Rewards Priority is the top-tier personal Southwest card, and at $229 per year, it's the priciest personal card in the Southwest lineup. The math got a little tighter in 2026 after the $75 travel credit was eliminated — but between the 7,500 anniversary points (~$97 value), complimentary seat selection at booking, unlimited Extra Legroom upgrades, and Group 5 boarding, there's still enough here to justify the fee for regular Southwest flyers.

This card is built for people who fly Southwest regularly and want the full suite of perks: choose your Preferred or Standard seat when you book (not just before departure), get bumped to Extra Legroom within 48 hours for free, earn the highest rate on Southwest purchases (4x), and pocket the biggest anniversary points bonus of any personal Southwest card. It's the premium Southwest experience for the assigned-seating era.

The Companion Pass qualifying points boost (10,000/year) is the same across all three Southwest cards, so the Priority's advantage lies in the seat perks, earning rates, anniversary points and faster A-List progress (2,500 tier qualifying points per $5,000 spent vs 1,500 on the Premier). If you don't fly often enough to take advantage of the seat selection and Extra Legroom upgrades, the Plus or Premier might be smarter.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• Complimentary Seat Selection at Booking: Choose a Preferred or Standard seat when you book, at no extra charge, for yourself and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation. This is the Priority card's marquee perk in Southwest's new assigned-seating world.
  • Unlimited Extra Legroom Upgrades: Upgrade to an Extra Legroom seat within 48 hours of departure, at no cost, when available — for you and up to 8 companions on the same reservation. No cap on how many times you use this per year.
  • 7,500 Anniversary Points: Worth roughly $97 in Southwest flights. This is the biggest offset against the $229 annual fee.
  • Group 5 Boarding: You and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation board no later than Group 5, giving you early access to overhead bins.
  • First Checked Bag Free: For the cardmember and up to 8 passengers on the same reservation. Same as the other Southwest cards.
  • 25% Back on Inflight Purchases: Statement credit on inflight drinks bought with your card. (Wi-Fi is already free for Rapid Rewards members.)
  • 10,000 Companion Pass QP Boost: Same as all Southwest cards — annual head start toward the Companion Pass.
  • 2,500 TQPs per $5K Spend: Earn tier qualifying points toward A-List status for every $5,000 in spending.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
• Annual Fee: $229 — effectively ~$132 after the 7,500 anniversary points ($97 value). You'll need to extract value from the seat selection and Extra Legroom perks to close the remaining gap.
  • Foreign Transaction Fees: None
  • APR: Variable, 19.24% - 27.74%
  • Balance Transfer Fee: 5% of the amount transferred, $5 minimum
  • Late Payment Fee: Up to $40

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
The standard offer is 60,000 bonus points after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first 3 months. At ~1.3 cents per point, that's roughly $780 in Southwest flight value — enough for 3-5 round-trip domestic flights.

The $2,000 spend requirement is very manageable — under $700/month. This makes it one of the easier premium card bonuses to earn. One catch: the card isn't available if you currently hold any personal Southwest card, or if you've received a Southwest card bonus in the last 24 months (Southwest business cards don't count).

Watch for limited-time offers that include the Companion Pass — these pop up periodically and are the single best promotion in the credit card world. A Companion Pass lets a designated companion fly with you for free (just taxes) for up to 14 months.

sections.title: Earning Rates
sections.content:
• 4x points on: Southwest Airlines purchases. The highest rate among personal Southwest cards.
  • 2x points on: Gas stations and restaurants.
  • 1x points on: Everything else.

The 4x on Southwest is solid — if you spend $2,000/year on Southwest flights, that's 8,000 points (~$104 value) from the bonus category alone. The 2x on gas and restaurants is decent but not category-leading. Note that the cards no longer earn 2x on Rapid Rewards Hotels, car rental partners, internet, cable, phone, streaming, or local transit — those categories were removed in the 2025 card refresh. For non-Southwest and non-restaurant spending, you're better off using a general rewards card like Freedom Unlimited or Citi Double Cash.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
Same as all Southwest cards — points redeem for Southwest flights with no blackout dates, no seat restrictions, and revenue-based pricing.

  • Southwest Flights: Points cover the fare at ~1.2-1.5 cents per point. No award charts to game.
  • Partner Airlines: Not a redemption option. Southwest's international partners (Icelandair, EVA Air, Turkish and others) are for connecting itineraries booked through the partner, not for spending your points.
  • Hotels & Car Rentals: Available but generally poor value compared to flights.
  • Gift Cards: Available but terrible value. Don't do this.

The beauty of Southwest points is simplicity. No blackout dates, no complicated charts, no devaluation drama. You know exactly what you're getting.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
• Complimentary Seat Selection at Booking: Pick a Preferred or Standard seat when you book — for you and up to 8 companions on the same reservation. This is the Priority card's biggest differentiator now that Southwest has moved to assigned seating.
  • Unlimited Extra Legroom Upgrades: Upgrade to Extra Legroom within 48 hours of departure, for free, when available. No annual cap. Covers you plus up to 8 passengers.
  • Group 5 Boarding: Board no later than Group 5 with up to 8 companions on the same reservation, giving you earlier access to overhead bin space.
  • 7,500 Anniversary Points: ~$97 in value, automatically deposited.
  • 25% Inflight Credit: Covers a quarter of your inflight drink costs (Wi-Fi is already free for Rapid Rewards members).
  • 2,500 TQPs per $5K: A path to A-List status through spending, which gets you Group 1 boarding and free same-day standby.

sections.title: Competitor Comparison
sections.content:
• vs. Southwest Premier ($149/yr): Save $80 but lose the complimentary seat selection at booking and the Extra Legroom upgrades, and get 1,500 fewer anniversary points and 3x (vs 4x) on Southwest. In return, the Premier gives you a 15% flight promo code every cardmember anniversary (excludes Basic fares), which the Priority doesn't offer. The Priority is worth the upgrade if you fly Southwest 4+ times a year and value picking your seat upfront.
  • vs. Southwest Plus ($99/yr): The Plus saves $130 but has weaker perks — 2x on Southwest (vs 4x), only 3,000 anniversary points, no seat selection at booking, no Extra Legroom upgrades. Only makes sense for very occasional flyers.
  • vs. Delta SkyMiles Platinum ($350/yr): More expensive, but it adds an annual Companion Certificate and a Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit. The right pick depends on your airline loyalty — both are solid mid-tier airline cards.
  • vs. United Quest ($350/yr): Pricier, but it comes with a $200 United travel credit and 2 free checked bags. Again, airline preference drives this decision.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:
• Frequent Southwest flyers: If you're on Southwest 5+ times a year, the seat selection and Extra Legroom perks alone justify the fee.
  • Companion Pass hunters: The 10,000 QP boost plus a big welcome bonus gets you closer to the 135,000-point threshold.
  • Families flying Southwest: Free first checked bags and seat selection for up to 9 people on the same reservation makes family travel far less chaotic.
  • A-List aspirants: The TQP earning from spending creates a viable path to A-List status.

Not ideal for: Occasional Southwest flyers (the Plus is cheaper), or travelers who fly multiple airlines (a flexible card like Sapphire Reserve is smarter).

title: Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier
scouts_verdict: The Southwest Premier is the sensible middle child of the Southwest card family. At $149, it gives you 3x on Southwest, 6,000 anniversary points, a 15% promo code (vs. 10%), and Preferred seating — meaningful upgrades over the $99 Plus card. But the $229 Priority card's seat selection at booking, free Extra Legroom upgrades and 4x on Southwest can be worth the extra $80 if you fly often. The Premier is best for moderate Southwest flyers who want more than the basics but don't fly enough to justify the Priority.
